paragraphs.text: The small harbour town is quiet for most of the year, but in summer it fills with visitors who come to walk along the cliffs and eat fresh fish in the restaurants by the water. Boats take tourists out to see the seals that rest on the rocks beyond the point, and in the evenings people gather on the quay to watch the sun go down behind the distant islands.

Clocks in public squares once played an important role in daily life, telling people when to open their shops, when to go to church and when to finish work. Before most people owned a watch, the sound of the bells could be heard across the whole town. Many of these old clocks still keep good time today, cared for by volunteers who climb the towers every week to wind them.

The forest path climbs gently for the first hour, passing between tall beech trees whose leaves form a green roof overhead. After crossing a small stream on a wooden footbridge, it becomes steeper and rockier, winding up toward a viewpoint where walkers can rest and look out over the valley. On clear days the snow-capped peaks on the far side are visible, shining in the afternoon light.

Bread ovens in old villages were often shared by the whole community. Families would prepare their dough at home and carry it to the oven early in the morning, marking each loaf so that they could recognise their own. While the bread baked, people chatted and exchanged news, so the oven became a meeting place as much as a kitchen. Some villages have restored their ovens and bake together on festival days.

Village festivals in late summer often begin with a procession through the main street, led by a band and followed by children in costumes and decorated wagons. Afterwards there are games on the green, stalls selling local food and a dance in the evening that goes on until long after dark. For people who have moved away, the festival is often the one weekend of the year when they come home to see old friends.

In the old part of the city, narrow lanes wind between tall houses whose upper floors almost touch above the street. Small workshops still occupy many of the ground floors, where craftsmen repair shoes, make jewellery or bind books by hand. Tourists wander through the lanes with maps, often getting lost, while residents carry their shopping home past the same doorways they have known all their lives.
